background: A designer is building a board game called Lantern Walk and has three ways for players to take turns. In **Alternating turns** players go one at a time, clockwise, over eight rounds. In **Simultaneous turns** everyone plans at once and reveals together, over six rounds. In **Bid for turn order** players bid each round for who goes first, over eight rounds, with two extra minutes of setup. The example is fictional, made to show how a design playtest reads as a report.

Four playtesters who know the designer played each version at a table of two and at a table of four. They rated how enjoyable each was (Dull, Okay, Fun, Great), the designer timed each session, the testers said which of two versions they would rather play again, and each ranked all three.
story.intent: The designer asked: “Which turn structure should the next prototype of Lantern Walk use?” They wanted the one players like most, as long as a session stays under 45 minutes.
questions: Which turn structure do playtesters rank first at a table of two, and at a table of four?
Does any structure make a session run longer than 45 minutes?
Do enjoyment ratings and head-to-head choices agree with the rankings?
story.rule: Fixed before playtesting: carry forward the version most playtesters rank first at each table size, unless its sessions run past 45 minutes; then carry the best-ranked version under 45 minutes. If the two table sizes carry different versions, carry both.

alternatives.alt: Alternating turns: one player at a time, clockwise, eight rounds, four minutes of setup. The current design, and the reference the others are measured against.
alternatives.sim: Simultaneous turns: everyone plans at once and reveals together, six rounds, four minutes of setup.
alternatives.bid: Bid for turn order: players bid each round for who goes first, eight rounds, six minutes of setup.

cases.two: A table of two players: the game's smallest table, where waiting for others matters least.
cases.four: A table of four players: the largest table, where turn order and waiting matter most and sessions run longest.

story.covers: Enjoyment ratings, session times, head-to-head choices and full rankings from four playtesters at two table sizes.
story.notCovered: Strangers or new players, three-player tables, how each version plays after many sessions, and the rules' clarity. One four-player session of Simultaneous turns was not timed because the stopwatch was not started.

glossary.meaning: The average position a version was ranked in; 1 is first, so lower is better.
How often one version's rating beats another's, minus how often it loses, halved: 0 means no lean either way.

decision.headline: The rule carries **Simultaneous turns** forward at both table sizes, but the four-player table preferred **Bid for turn order**, which runs too long.
detail: At two players both testers ranked Simultaneous turns first and its sessions ran 22 and 25 minutes. At four players three of four ranked Bid for turn order first and rated it Great, but its sessions ran 52 and 49 minutes, past the 45-minute limit, so the rule passes to the best-ranked variant under the limit: Simultaneous turns, at 31 minutes.
The preference for bidding at four players is the finding the rule does not carry, and the testers' words say why.
conditions: Four playtesters who know the designer, at a table of two and a table of four
Ratings and rankings given after all three variants were played in one sitting
limits: Four people: rankings are counted, not averaged, and no count is large enough to call a difference.
The variants were played in the same order at every table, so learning may favor the one played last, Bid for turn order.
One four-player session of Simultaneous turns was not timed, so its length rests on a single session.
changes: Trimming Bid for turn order to six rounds so it fits the slot, then testing it at four players again

readings.compared: Three turn structures for the same game: alternating, simultaneous and bidding. They differ in how turns are taken, the number of rounds and setup time, as the table shows.
readings.results: Simultaneous turns and Bid for turn order were rated Fun at the median, Alternating turns Okay. Simultaneous turns ran shortest, 26 minutes on average, against about 47 for the other two. Bid for turn order had the best mean rank (1.83, where 1 is first), but with four testers every interval overlaps.
readings.differences: Against Alternating turns, Simultaneous sessions were 21.5 minutes shorter (interval −43.6 to +0.6 minutes, just short of clear). No difference in enjoyment, head-to-head choice or ranking clears zero: four testers cannot separate the three on liking alone.
readings.cases: The two table sizes disagree. At two players both testers ranked Simultaneous turns first and won all its decisive head-to-head choices; at four players three of four ranked Bid for turn order first and rated it Great, but its sessions ran 52 and 49 minutes, past the 45-minute limit.
readings.judgments: Head to head over both tables, Bid for turn order won 6 of 11 decisive choices, Simultaneous 5 of 10 and Alternating 5 of 11; all of Bid's wins came at the four-player table, where it beat both others.
readings.observations: Thirty ratings and times; one is invalid, the untimed four-player session of Simultaneous turns.
